description: A solo team interested in engaging with SAR and GEOSINT.
summary:
Arctic communities rely on narrow waterways for essential resupply. Freeze-up events can obstruct these passages, while drifting icebergs may disrupt shipping routes. Follow the Ice transforms repeated NASA–ISRO NISAR and Copernicus Sentinel‑1 radar observations into an interactive atlas, enabling researchers and maritime planners to monitor freeze-up, glacier motion, rift formation, and iceberg drift under cloud cover and during polar night.

During four NISAR passes in October 2026, iceberg A‑84 was tracked, revealing 26.5 km of drift over 37 hours between the final two passes (0.72 km/h). A retrospective calving scenario estimated that 380.3 km² of ice could detach. The predicted footprint achieved 82% intersection over union with the 460.6 km² reconstructed loss. Additionally, an experimental alert surpassed its threshold eight days prior to calving in the replay.

In a D‑33 eisberg case, our pixel detector achieved 99.2% balanced accuracy on approximately labelled pixels, compared to 98.9% for a fixed brightness threshold. The prototype demonstrates how new radar observations can update object histories and flag changes for subsequent human review.
details:
Explore Follow the Ice

GitHub repository

How it works

Follow a glacier, iceberg, or region of sea ice through dated observations. We align NASA–ISRO NISAR and Copernicus Sentinel‑1 radar on shared map grids. The atlas combines speckle filtering, interferograms, a raster calculator, candidate iceberg masks, and drift measurements. Optical scenes, ice charts, and weather help interpret changes in the radar signal. The time series show each acquisition, its source, and where the evidence is uncertain.

Our computer-vision prototype flags bright iceberg pixels using local brightness and texture. On 16,594 approximately labelled pixels in a held-out D‑33 scene, it reached 99.2% balanced accuracy. A fixed brightness threshold reached 98.9% on the same pixels. Tests on independently labelled scenes and darker ice are future work.

Follow the Ice architecture · Explore the interactive diagram

Use cases

Flag potential iceberg calving

Glaciologists can follow the widening of an ice-shelf rift across repeat radar passes, flag accelerated opening for review, and estimate how much ice could detach.

In a retrospective test at A‑84, a scenario drawn from a 30 November 2024 Sentinel‑1A scene extended the mapped rift by 19.1 km and estimated a potential break-off area of 380.3 km². The 17 January 2025 radar scene showed a reconstructed loss of 460.6 km², with 82% intersection over union. A separate alert experiment fitted on Pine Island B‑49 data used manually measured rift width and opening rate. In this single retrospective test, it crossed its threshold eight days before the reported A‑84 calving.

A‑84 calving scenario and reconstructed loss from Sentinel‑1A radar.

Nansen Ice Shelf. In a second retrospective test, a 40.7 km² calving outline reached 90% intersection over union with the 44.5 km² reconstructed loss. Nansen Story

Track iceberg drift and estimate speed

Ice analysts can match an iceberg across repeat radar passes to measure distance, direction, and average speed. The measurements help analysts check whether an iceberg is moving toward a shipping route or another area of interest.

Four NISAR observations from October 2026 follow A‑84 after calving. Between the final two passes, it moved about 26.5 km in 37 hours, averaging about 0.72 km/h.

A‑84 on 31 October 2026. The overlay marks the detected iceberg, its outline, and the path traced by its positions across radar passes.

Watch the A‑84 drift GIF · 26–31 October 2026

B‑52. NISAR shows B‑52 turning and drifting after separation near the Getz Ice Shelf. Sentinel‑2 imagery and U.S. National Ice Center records helped verify its outline and position. B‑52 Story · B‑52 radar GIF

Follow iceberg fragments after breakup

Petermann Glacier. We matched a GPS beacon to six NISAR views after the iceberg fragmented. In Lancaster Sound, beacon positions at the first and last passes were 110.65 km apart over about 43 hours and 22 minutes. Petermann GPS timeline

D‑33. We tracked fragments D‑33A and D‑33D separately. On 21 July 2026, D‑33D’s radar outline covered about 158 km². It averaged 3.1 km/day between the final two measured positions. D‑33 Timeline

Check ice conditions in a narrow passage

Maritime planners and local observers can compare satellite observations to see how much open water remains near a glacier front and where ice may restrict a resupply passage. Radar provides observations through cloud cover and darkness, and daylight imagery helps interpret the scene when available.

At Hubbard Glacier, the atlas combines radar and daylight observations of the narrow passage into Russell Fjord near Gilbert Point.

Hubbard Glacier and Russell Fjord in NISAR radar and Sentinel‑2 daylight imagery, 24 August 2026.

Radar and daylight observations near Gilbert Point.

Measure glacier motion

Belcher Glacier. NISAR pixel offsets showed about 7.7 m of along-track movement in a marked ice patch over 12 days. Belcher Story

Sermeq Kujalleq. During polar night, NISAR pixel offsets showed about 4.9 m of along-track movement at a marked point over 24 days. Sermeq Story

Monitor seasonal sea-ice change

Ice analysts can compare repeat radar passes to see where sea ice forms and breaks up. Ice charts and weather at acquisition time help interpret changes in radar brightness.

In Amundsen Gulf, the atlas compares NISAR observations from September and October 2026 alongside dated ice charts and weather at acquisition time.

Amundsen Gulf before and during freeze-up in NISAR HH radar, 13 September and 31 October 2026.

Cambridge Bay. At the selected point on Canadian Ice Service charts, ice concentration fell from 90% to under 10% from 6 to 13 July 2026. Cambridge Bay Story

Dolphin and Union Strait. At the selected chart point, ice concentration rose from about 50% to 90–100% from 2 to 9 November 2026. Dolphin and Union Strait Story

Next steps

  1. Automate data updates. Collect new radar scenes and update the time series for each tracked zone.
  2. Develop early calving alerts. Show when calving could occur and send proactive alerts.
  3. Work with InSAR coherence gaps. Identify when phase measurements are reliable. Use radar intensity or feature tracking when phase coverage is too sparse.

Use of Super Intelligence

We used AI assistance to write and debug code and to improve project texts.
